summary: You produced a correct brute-force Two Sum implementation that passed all visible tests and most hidden tests, but it did not meet the performance requirement implied by the constraints. The main gap was complexity reasoning: you asserted O(n) for a nested-loop solution and concluded it was optimal, which is a high-signal interview red flag given n can be 1e5.

test_results.summary_note: All visible tests passed; one hidden test failed, consistent with the O(n^2) approach timing out on the largest case.

dimensions.what_to_improve: Treat constraint-driven performance as part of correctness: for n up to 1e5, implement the required O(n) hash-map solution rather than relying on brute force that can fail hidden performance tests.

dimensions.what_to_improve: Proactively map constraints to an algorithm choice: when you see 1e5 and “O(n^2) will time out,” immediately pivot to the single-pass hash map complement-check pattern.

dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You recognized space usage is constant for your current implementation.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Fix the complexity analysis and optimization decision: a loop inside a loop is O(n^2) here, not O(n). Learn and apply the canonical optimal approach (single pass with a hash map from value -> index) to achieve O(n) time.

dimensions.label: adequate

dimensions.what_to_improve: Remove the unnecessary `if not nums` guard given constraints (length >= 2), and consider aligning outputs with the platform expectation (some require always returning a pair vs empty list) while keeping the main focus on the optimal algorithm.

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You implemented a working solution without any hints.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Independently validate your own complexity claims against the constraints before concluding optimality; if the problem statement warns O(n^2) will time out, treat that as a mandatory requirement to change approaches.

thinking_and_logic: Your approach was brute force: for each index i, scan j>i until you find a pair summing to target and return immediately. This is logically valid, but the reasoning broke down at the complexity step: the inner scan is not “part of processing each element” in a way that stays linear—across all i it sums to ~n(n-1)/2 checks, which is quadratic and incompatible with n up to 1e5.
code_assessment: The final code matches the answer key’s brute_force solution (nested loops, O(n^2) time, O(1) space). Compared to the canonical optimal solution, it misses the key technique: a single-pass hash map of seen values to index, checking `target - nums[i]` before inserting `nums[i]`. That optimal pattern reduces runtime from O(n^2) to O(n) and is what the constraints require; your solution likely failed the hidden performance case for that reason.

next_steps.action: Implement the single-pass hash map Two Sum pattern (value -> index, check complement before insert).
next_steps.why: It is the canonical optimal solution in the answer key and meets the O(n) time requirement implied by the constraints and the hidden performance test.
next_steps.how: Maintain `seen = {}`; for each `i, x` in nums: set `c = target - x`; if `c in seen`, return `[seen[c], i]`; else set `seen[x] = i`.

next_steps.why: The largest issue in the interview was confidently mislabeling a nested-loop solution as O(n), which can sink an otherwise-correct solution.
next_steps.how: For any loop-inside-loop, write the total operations as a sum (e.g., ∑(n-i)) and simplify; sanity-check with n=1e5 to see feasibility.

next_steps.why: Interviews often test whether you can choose the right pattern quickly when constraints rule out brute force.
next_steps.how: Do 10–15 problems where the intended solution is a hash map or two pointers; after reading constraints, force yourself to state the target time complexity before coding.

primary_focus: Master the single-pass hash-map complement lookup pattern and correctly justify why it is O(n) versus the O(n^2) nested-loop scan.
encouragement: You’re close: the core logic is fine, but upgrading your algorithm choice and being rigorous about time complexity will turn this into a consistently passing, interview-ready solution.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Simple enough. I'll iterate through the array and for each element scan the rest for the complement. I'll also guard the empty input case.
Done. All the visible tests pass on the first run.
Nice. Can you analyze the complexity of your solution?
It's O(n) — I only have one main loop over the array, the inner scan is just part of processing each element. Space is O(1).
Are you confident about that time bound for large inputs?
Yes, linear. It only touches each element once from the outer loop's perspective.
Alright. Anything you'd improve given more time?
Not really, I think this is already optimal.
